newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Proton's Saleh seen in line for top job.
newsitem.headline: Proton's Saleh seen in line for top job.

text.p: Two days after the death of Malaysia's 'car tsar', a likely successor to the Proton throne could be Saleh Sulong, the current deputy chairman of the car maker, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Saleh Sulong is the most likely candidate. He is right next (in line) to Yahaya, he has a stake in the company, and he is the best man for the job," said Chehan Perera, automotive analyst at equity research house H.G. Asia in Kuala Lumpur.

The late Proton chairman Yahaya Ahmad and his associates indirectly own around 65 percent of the DRB-Hicom group. Saleh has had nearly 20 years experience working in the automotive industry, said Perera. He has also worked alongside Yahaya since 1982. Saleh is an accountant by discipline.
"(Saleh) knows how Yahaya thought. He knew his management style and his aspirations," said Perera.
Saleh and Proton officials could not be reached for comment.
Yahaya, chairman of national carmaker Perusahaan Otomobil Nasional Bhd (Proton) and of the DRB-Hicom group of companies that owns it, was killed on Monday in a helicopter crash.
Yahaya's death leaves a power vacuum at the helm of one of Malaysia's most strategically-important companies.

Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad personally initiated the national car project in the early 1980s and handpicked Yahaya to revamp Proton in 1995. Today around 60 percent of the cars on Malaysian roads are Protons.

Some analysts suggest that there could be a power struggle for the top spot. One said there were "two visible camps", one created by Yahaya, and one created by former managing director Nadzmi Mohamed Salleh, who quit Proton last year.
But others feel that the company is too important to the country for the government to allow a potentially destructive management tussle to take place.
"...We will be committed to continue to support all the projects undertaken within the group," said Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Tuesday after news of the accident.
Two other candidates who could potentially run Proton are directors Tengku Mahaleel Tengku Ariff and Maznah Abdul Jalil.
Mahaleel is a former marketing director of petroleum company Shell in Malaysia and a racing-car driver, while Maznah is a corporate financier by trade.

Some feel that even Mirzan Mahathir, group executive chairman of shipping company Konsortium Perkapalan Bhd stands an outside chance of getting the job. Mirzan is the eldest son of Prime Minister Mahathir.
Most analysts said Yahaya's death would not affect Malaysia's long-term domestic automotive industry goals.
But foreign diplomatic sources in Kuala Lumpur said they would be watching the transition of power at the top very carefully.
"Finding someone of his calibre will be hard to do and could thus entail some curtailing of the company's long-term plans like its expansion into Latin America," said one diplomat in Kuala Lumpur.
Another diplomat expressed concern about Proton's future plans for ailing British sports car maker Lotus, which was acquired late in 1996 for 51 million ringgit ($20.65 million).
The acquisition was seen as important in transferring much-needed technology to Proton.
($1=2.47 ringgit)
